content: Sputum smear-positive new patients are included in the survey, while those who are smear-negative are excluded. Very small health centers with a low number of reported cases may not achieve the target sample size, necessitating alternative approaches. For instance, if the minimum recommended number of 30 clusters is selected, the total number of patients registered annually across all centers is divided by 30 to determine the sampling interval. A random number between 1 and the sampling interval is chosen, denoted as x. Using the cumulative case count, the diagnostic center corresponding to the xth patient is selected as the first cluster. The sampling interval is then sequentially added to the random number to identify the remaining clusters from the list. In large centers with two to three times more patients per year than the average, the sampling interval may be smaller than the total patient intake for these centers. In such cases, more than one cluster may be selected from these centers. For example, if a center is chosen twice, contributing two clusters, the sample size for that center will be double that of a center serving as only one cluster. To calculate the number of patients per cluster, the required total sample size is divided by the number of clusters. In all selected health centers, consecutive patients are enrolled in the survey until the required number of new cases is reached. For each new survey, clusters must be reselected using the most recent TB notification data, as clusters from a previous survey cannot be assumed to represent the current situation. For example, if a sample size of 360 new TB patients is calculated, accounting for the effect of cluster sampling, 30 clusters of 12 new patients each (360/30) are selected. The following steps are taken: 1. A list of health centers with their annual number of patients is established. 2. The cumulative number of new patients is calculated and recorded in an additional column. For instance, the cumulative number for the second center is the sum of the first and second centers' patient numbers, and so on. The total number of patients diagnosed in the country is 6,322. 3. The sampling interval is determined by dividing 6,322 by 30, resulting in 211. 4. A random number between 0 and 211 is selected (e.g., 120). 5. The first cluster is selected using the random number 120, which falls within the range of 0 to 246 (the number of patients in the first center). 6. Subsequent clusters are selected by adding the sampling interval of 211 to the first number (120). For example, the next number (120 + 211 = 331) falls between 246 and 1,823 (the cumulative number of patients for the second center), so the second cluster is selected in the second center. The third number (331 + 211 = 542) also falls within this range, so the third cluster is also selected in the second center. Small health centers with fewer than ten new cases per year may not meet the required sample size. If such centers are rare, they can be excluded from the sampling frame before cluster selection. However, if small centers are common, their exclusion may introduce selection bias. In this case, neighboring small centers should be grouped together and treated as a single unit in the sampling frame. If a group is selected as a cluster, all centers in the group must contribute to the target cluster sample size by enrolling consecutive patients. This requires effective communication and coordination among the centers within the same cluster. The budget for the survey must be carefully calculated to avoid interruptions during implementation. All necessary funds for the entire survey period (planning, implementation, analysis, and dissemination) must be secured before starting. National TB control programs should view surveys not only as a means of estimating the magnitude of drug resistance but also as a tool for monitoring program efficiency and strengthening the capacity of the Central Reference Laboratory to perform drug susceptibility testing (DST). The allocation of funds for surveys should be an integral part of the program's budget. The average cost of nationwide surveys is approximately $250,000–$300,000, based on a sample size of 1,000–1,500 patients. Costs may vary depending on laboratory methods and country-specific logistics, such as transportation distances. Budgets requiring the services of Supranational Reference Laboratories (SRLs) should include costs for technical assistance, retesting isolates, laboratory work, and specimen shipment for quality assessment. Additional costs may include staffing for specimen processing and laboratory operations. Coordination costs, such as staff salaries, monitoring meetings, supervisory visits, and communication between peripheral centers and the central laboratory, should also be included. Training is essential for survey implementation and should focus on patient enrollment, specimen collection and transportation, data collection forms, laboratory techniques, communication of results, and data entry and analysis. Training activities should involve all health workers directly participating in the survey. Medical officers and nurses responsible for patient intake and interviews should be properly instructed. Training or refresher courses at peripheral laboratories should cover sample registration, smear preparation and reading, molecular testing methods, sputum decontamination for culture, sample storage and transport, and result recording. Laboratory preparedness is critical. Staff from the Central Reference Laboratory should visit peripheral laboratories before the survey to ensure internal quality control procedures are in place. Sputum collection, smear examination, and transport must be carefully supervised. Surveys may place significant pressure on laboratories, so logistics, facilities, and resources must be planned in advance to prevent overwhelming the laboratory network. A quality assurance system, including internal quality control and external quality assessment, should be established before the survey. Biosafety measures must also be in place. The partner SRL can provide guidance during planning, implementation, and evaluation. Before the survey, experienced SRL staff should assess the Central Reference Laboratory's standard operating procedures, performance, quality assurance, and biosafety. SRLs can also train staff if needed. A pilot study in selected sites can test the entire survey process, including patient identification, sputum collection, laboratory testing, documentation, and coordination. This helps identify and resolve unexpected issues before full implementation. If no significant problems arise during the pilot, the data collected can contribute to the survey's sample size. Survey logistics depend on inclusion and exclusion criteria and the diagnostic testing algorithm. Inclusion criteria are defined based on the survey objectives. New patients who started TB treatment more than one week earlier are excluded to avoid bias, as they may harbor drug-resistant strains. Previously treated smear-positive cases are included only if they are beginning a new treatment course, such as relapse or treatment after loss to follow-up. Treatment failure patients are included only if their first treatment course failed. Subsequent treatment failures are excluded. Children under 15 meeting the criteria should be included, with parental consent as required by local laws. Extrapulmonary TB and smear-negative cases are usually excluded due to diagnostic challenges and resource limitations, though their inclusion may be feasible with advanced diagnostic methods like Xpert MTB/RIF. Each patient enrolled in the survey is assigned a unique identification number linked to their data. This ensures accurate data collection and patient identification, particularly in cases of drug-resistant strains or when additional information is needed. All eligible patients should be enrolled and provide sputum samples before starting treatment. The number of samples required depends on the diagnostic methods used. Regular comparison of eligible and enrolled patients can help identify reasons for non-enrollment and reduce the likelihood of missing eligible patients.
